We need to stop mixing words across domains, and rather invent new ones, as this is all making us confused.

"Seems to be self aware" here  means that the model exhibits behavior that compares with behavior of other self aware agents (humans). When we use this vocabulary, we unconsciously imply other traits to the models, since the only other agent that we know is self aware is us (leaving animals out of it for simplicity). We are terrible at separating metaphors or analogies to what we are referencing, so once we accept the word "self aware" for AI models, even if just to metaphorically describe behavior, we open up to mixing up the metaphor with the real deal with no theoretical reason to do so. We also prime ourselves to accepting even more traits relating to, not the AI model, but the metaphor we used to describe its behavior. Thos soon leads people to accept that models can likely be or become sentient, conscious, have inner mental lives etc. None of it supported by any science of course.

A few things are crucial to remember - we are describing behavior of models operating in domains humans otherwise operate in, which which leaves us vulnerable to antropomorphizing their behavior. We are also describing models that are trained or constructed to operate in, or communicate through, ways shared by humans, which again invites antropomorphizing the result. Lastly, there is NO scientific backing for consciousness emerging from compute in any form, in humans, animals nor AI models. While its fun thoughts to play with, we must do so as we play w science fiction stories, but there is literally no evidence (or even viable theory) that suggests that consciousness appears through emergence or some vague "complexity".

We interpret and describe behavior, through a human perspective, using metaphors, and then forget we did so. I will leave it with a quote from Bernardo Kastrup, "even a perfectly simulated kidney won't pee on my desk".
